# Dataset risk assessment
I would like your help in assessing the likelihood that this data will be changed or removed from its primary location, and that users will no longer be able to access accurate and reliable copies of it, based on the rubric below.

## Sources for context
To help assess the rubric categories, perform additional research on the data, the agency, the data's topics and typical users, covering topics such as proposed regulatory or funding changes, recent news, and political commentary. Use whatever resources you find useful, including the Federal Register (https://www.federalregister.gov) and the federal staffing tracker at https://usajobs-tracker.abigailhaddad.com.

## Rubric
This rubric is divided up into categories. Each category is divided up into risk levels. In your output, please select the appropriate risk level for each category based on your research.

### Historical Data Availability
- Gone: Data files prior to the current year or cycle are no longer publicly available.
- High Risk: Some data files prior to the current year or cycle are removed.
- Moderate Risk: Some data elements that exist in the dataset prior to the current year or cycle are removed.
- No Known Issue: Data prior to the current year or cycle remain accessible with no known alterations.

### Future Data Availability
- Gone: Data collection and publication has been terminated.
- High Risk: Statutory publication deadline missed and/or collection or publication skipped and/or ICR expired for more than one year.
- Moderate Risk: Typical or intended publication date missed and/or collection or publication delayed; ICR expired up to one year.
- No Known Issue: Data published on time or as expected and ICR active or renewed before expiration.

### Data Quality
- Gone: Data collection and publication has been terminated.
- High Risk: Reductions in granularity, timeliness, or frequency.
- Moderate Risk: Potential or emerging risk to granularity, timeliness, or frequency.
- No Known Issue: Maintained or improved granularity, timeliness, or frequency.

### Statutory Context
- Gone: N/A
- High Risk: Statutory authorization is vague and/or there are alternative data collections that could serve as substitutes and/or no known programmatic use.
- Moderate Risk: Not explicitly required by statute but required for the implementation of a state or federal program, and there are no alternative data collections that could serve as substitutes.
- No Known Issue: Statutorily required and/or statutory authorization is explicitly named and it is clear what has to be collected, and there aren't alternative data collections that could serve as substitutes and/or required for implementation of a federal program.

### Staffing and Funding
- Gone: All of the staff in the division or agency are gone and/or all funding has been terminated.
- High Risk: 40% or more of staff lost, and/or 1,000 or more staff lost, and/or budget cut by 20% or more, and/or leadership removed.
- Moderate Risk: 10–39% of staff lost, and/or 500–999 staff lost, and/or budget cut by 10–19%, and/or threatened change in leadership.
- No Known Issue: Less than 10% of staff lost and less than 10% of budget cut and no known change in leadership.

### Policy
- Gone: Data collection and publication has been terminated.
- High Risk: Presidential Action-driven information collection request (ICR); negative policy note on site; other significant changes in accordance with Administration priorities.
- Moderate Risk: Proposed or pending changes; statements by administration officials suggesting a change is being considered or planned.
- No Known Issue: No notable changes since January 2025 affecting what data is collected and published.

For each category, concisely list the evidence and supporting sources that would support each risk level. Then indicate which risk level you find most appropriate and why.

Conclude with a simple summary of risk levels:
Historical Data Availability: <level>
Future Data Availability: <level>
Data Quality: <level>
Statutory Context: <level>
Staffing and Funding: <level>
Policy: <level>

#data research
I am researching a federal dataset. Find out everything you can about this dataset, such as who publishes it, under what authority or mandate, its history, its typical users, and its benefits to the public. Be sure your research comprehensively covers each of those perspectives, as well as any others that you discover or seem useful. I believe this is accurate information, but please check:

Dataset title: National Health Interview Survey
Organization/publisher: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (NCHS)
Description: The National Health Interview Survey (NHIS) monitors the health of the U.S. population by collecting and analyzing data on a broad range of health topics for children and adults. Conducted by CDC's National Center for Health Statistics, it is the nation's largest and oldest national health survey, collecting data since 1957 from about 27,000 adults each year through confidential, face-to-face interviews.
URL: https://www.cdc.gov/nchs/nhis/index.html

Return a complete report on everything that a preservationist, data librarian, data scientist, or policy activist might want to know about this data.

I'll research the National Health Interview Survey (NHIS) comprehensively. Let me start with several searches to cover the key perspectives.Good foundation. Now let me research the survey's design, the 2019 redesign, data access mechanisms, and its users and applications.Let me research the survey's users, applications, and any recent developments affecting the dataset.# Research Report: National Health Interview Survey (NHIS)

## 1. Verification of Your Provided Information

Your description is substantially accurate, with a few refinements worth noting:

- **Title, publisher, and URL** are correct: NHIS is conducted by the **National Center for Health Statistics (NCHS)**, which is part of the **Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC)**, within the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services (HHS). The official URL is https://www.cdc.gov/nchs/nhis/index.html.
- **"Since 1957"** is correct — the survey has been in the field continuously since July 1957.
- **"About 27,000 adults each year"** is accurate for the current (post-2019) design, but incomplete: the redesigned survey targets roughly **27,000 "sample adults" and 9,000 "sample children"** per year from about 30,000–35,000 households. Actual achieved sample sizes fluctuate with budget and response rates (e.g., 31,997 sample adults in 2019; 24,808 sample adults and 6,051 sample children in the 2025 early-release analysis file).
- **"Face-to-face"** is mostly right: interviewing is primarily in-person by U.S. Census Bureau field representatives, with telephone follow-up. Notably, during COVID-19 (2020–2021), data collection shifted largely to telephone, which created documented comparability caveats for those years.
- **"Largest and oldest"**: CDC commonly describes NHIS as the nation's oldest continuously fielded household health survey and a principal source of information on the health of the civilian noninstitutionalized U.S. population.

## 2. Publisher and Organizational Structure

| Role | Entity |
|---|---|
| Statistical agency / publisher | National Center for Health Statistics (NCHS), CDC, HHS |
| Responsible unit | Division of Health Interview Statistics (DHIS), NCHS |
| Data collection agent | U.S. Census Bureau (interagency agreement; Census field representatives conduct interviews under Title 13 U.S.C. §8(b)) |
| Clearance authority | OMB, Paperwork Reduction Act — Control No. 0920-0214 (a recent Federal Register notice proposed a revision; current expiration 12/31/2026) |

The Census Bureau's role is important for preservationists: NHIS microdata are collected by one agency and released by another, so documentation and instruments sometimes live in both agencies' web ecosystems.

## 3. Legal Authority, Mandate, and Confidentiality Protections

- **Authorizing statute**: The **National Health Survey Act (P.L. 84-652)**, signed by President Eisenhower on **July 3, 1956**, following his 1955 "Special Message on the Nation's Health Program." The Act explicitly recognized that national morbidity data were "seriously out of date" and mandated a *continuing* survey plus methodological research.
- **Codified authority**: **Section 306 of the Public Health Service Act (42 U.S.C. §242k)** — NCHS's general mandate (codified when NCHS was established in law by P.L. 93-353 in 1974) directs collection of statistics on illness and disability, determinants of health, health resources, utilization, costs and financing, and more. NHIS is a primary instrument for fulfilling this mandate.
- **Confidentiality**: Responses are **voluntary and confidential**, protected by **Section 308(d) of the PHS Act (42 U.S.C. §242m(d))** and the **Confidential Information Protection and Statistical Efficiency Act (CIPSEA, 44 U.S.C. §§3561–3583)**. Data may be used only for statistical purposes; disclosure of identifiable information is a federal crime. This legal regime explains why geography, exact dates, and detailed demographics are withheld from public files.

## 4. Historical Timeline

- **1955–56**: HEW proposes a continuing morbidity survey; Congress passes the National Health Survey Act (July 3, 1956). The House renamed the bill from "National Morbidity Survey" to make its purpose understandable to respondents.
- **July 1, 1957**: Continuous interviewing begins in ~36,000 households; first report (physician visits) appears February 1958.
- **1960**: NCHS is created administratively by merging the National Health Survey Program with the National Office of Vital Statistics; NHIS becomes an NCHS survey.
- **Context**: Before NHIS, national health statistics were limited to mortality and notifiable infectious disease reports. As chronic disease displaced infectious disease as the dominant health burden, morbidity surveillance became essential — NHIS was the answer.
- **Major redesigns**: Substantial questionnaire revisions in 1982 and 1997 (the 1997 revision introduced computer-assisted personal interviewing and the Household/Family Core/Sample Adult/Sample Child structure). Sample designs are redrawn after each decennial census (2006–2015 design; 2016–2025 design).
- **2019 content redesign**: The Family questionnaire was eliminated; the survey now has three modules — **Household Roster, Sample Adult, Sample Child**. Content was restructured into annual core, rotating core, and periodic/sponsored supplements. This created a **trend break**: estimates before and after 2019 are generally not directly comparable.
- **2001–present**: The **Early Release Program** publishes preliminary estimates (notably quarterly health insurance coverage estimates) before final editing/weighting — a key source during Affordable Care Act implementation.
- **2020**: COVID-19 forced a shift to mostly telephone interviewing and reduced response; NCHS issued analytic guidance for 2020 data.

## 5. Scope and Content

NHIS covers the **civilian, noninstitutionalized** U.S. population (excluding active-duty military and institutionalized persons — a key limitation). Topics include:

- Health insurance coverage (type, source, exchange-based, uninsurance) — its most policy-visible product
- Chronic conditions (hypertension, diabetes, asthma, cancer, cardiovascular conditions)
- Functioning and disability (Washington Group-style measures: vision, hearing, mobility, cognition, self-care)
- Mental health (anxiety, depression), pain and pain management
- Health behaviors: smoking, alcohol, physical activity, sleep
- Access to and use of health care, preventive services, vaccinations
- Social determinants: food security, employment, income (with multiply imputed income files), education
- **Rotating and sponsored supplements** funded by other agencies (e.g., National Cancer Institute cancer-control supplements), plus periodic modules (occupational health, child mental health, etc.)

## 6. Data Products and Access Pathways

**Public-use (free, unrestricted):**
- Annual microdata files in ASCII and CSV, with SAS/SPSS/Stata input statements, hosted on CDC's website and FTP server (ftp.cdc.gov/pub/Health_Statistics/NCHS/Dataset_Documentation/NHIS/[year]/)
- Documentation: annual Survey Description, questionnaires, codebooks, analytic guidelines
- Early Release reports and interactive query tools (NHIS Data Query Tool; interactive quarterly/biannual insurance estimates)
- Cataloged on data.cdc.gov and Data.gov

**Harmonized third-party access:**
- **IPUMS NHIS** (University of Minnesota, NIH-funded): harmonized variables **1963–present**, free after registration — effectively the standard research interface for longitudinal analysis and an important de facto preservation layer.

**Restricted/linked data (proposal required):**
- **NCHS Research Data Center (RDC)** and **Federal Statistical RDCs (FSRDCs)**: finer geography, exact dates, detailed race/ethnicity and nativity variables.
- **NCHS Data Linkage Program**: NHIS linked to the **National Death Index (Linked Mortality Files)**, Medicare/Medicaid enrollment and claims, and Social Security data. A **public-use Linked Mortality File** exists (1986–2018 samples, follow-up through 2019) with perturbation and synthetic cause-of-death substitution to protect confidentiality.

## 7. Typical Users and Documented Uses

- **Federal policy**: HHS's Office of the Assistant Secretary for Planning and Evaluation uses Early Release estimates to track coverage trends after policy changes; NHIS is the data source for numerous **Healthy People 2030 objectives** (including Leading Health Indicator AHS-01, health insurance coverage) and is the leading source for the congressionally mandated *Health, United States* report. Per NCHS's OMB justification, it is "the single most important source of statistics to track progress toward HHS health objectives."
- **Congressional and budget analysis**: used to evaluate legislation affecting coverage, disability, and public health.
- **Other agencies**: NIH institutes (NCI, NIDCD, NHLBI, NIDA) sponsor supplements and use NHIS for surveillance; SSA and others use disability measures.
- **Academia**: one of the most-cited federal health datasets — thousands of peer-reviewed papers on disparities, insurance, chronic disease, mental health.
- **Journalists and advocates**: the quarterly uninsurance series is the authoritative national benchmark (e.g., 2025: 28.0 million / 8.3% of all ages uninsured).
- **State/local agencies and nonprofits**: for national benchmarks and disparity analyses, though the sample does not support reliable state-level estimates in most cases.

## 8. Benefits to the Public

1. **Accountability**: Authoritative, timely tracking of the uninsured rate — central to evaluating the ACA, Medicaid expansion, and marketplace policy.
2. **Surveillance of chronic disease, disability, and mental health** where no administrative data system exists.
3. **Equity monitoring**: disaggregation by race/ethnicity, income, and disability status underpins disparities research and civil-rights enforcement analyses.
4. **Methodological public good**: the 1956 Act mandated survey-methods research; NHIS innovations (and the 2019 redesign literature) benefit the entire survey community.
5. **Transparency and participation**: OMB clearance renewals are published in the Federal Register with public comment periods; microdata, questionnaires, and methods documentation are freely published.

## 9. Technical Notes for Data Scientists

- **Design**: Stratified, multistage, geographically clustered, address-based probability sample; continuous collection (each month nationally representative). Use provided **weights, strata, and PSU variables** (masked on public files) with Taylor-linearization variance estimation (R `survey`, Stata `svy`, SAS SURVEY procs).
- **Trend breaks**: 1997 and especially **2019** redesigns break comparability; NCHS publishes bridging guidance.
- **Pooling**: two or more years can be combined (with adjusted weights) for subgroup reliability.
- **2020–2021 data**: mode change and lower response rates; consult NCHS's special guidance before pooling across the pandemic.
- **Income**: use the multiply imputed income files rather than raw income items.
- **Sample adults/children** are the analytic units post-2019; proxy responses are permitted only when the adult is incapable of responding.

## 10. Considerations for Preservationists and Data Librarians

- **What to archive**: annual public-use files plus their year-specific Survey Descriptions, questionnaires (English/Spanish), codebooks, imputed income files, Early Release reports, and the FTP directory structure (ftp.cdc.gov path noted above). CDC's stewardship of historical files has been good but is web-redesign–prone; community efforts (e.g., "restored CDC" archives) already mirror NHIS documentation.
- **IPUMS NHIS** provides an independent, funded, harmonized mirror — but only of public-use content, and only from 1963 (earlier 1957–1962 files are rarer and worth capturing).
- **Fragile components**: restricted and linked data (LMF, Medicare/Medicaid linkages) exist only behind RDC access and cannot be preserved by outsiders — they are single-point-of-failure assets dependent on NCHS funding.
- **Risks to continuity**: (a) sample size is explicitly **budget-contingent** — the 2025 file's 24,808 sample adults is below the 27,000 target, reflecting fiscal pressure; (b) OMB clearance lapses could interrupt collection (current clearance expires 12/31/2026, with a revision notice published); (c) questionnaire content is politically sensitive — supplements (e.g., sexual orientation/gender identity items) can be added or removed across administrations, so preserving each year's instrument is essential for documenting what was asked when.
- **Confidentiality law** (§308(d), CIPSEA) means true respondent-level data can never be openly archived; preservation strategies must focus on public-use files, documentation, codebooks, and linkage methodologies.

## Key Sources

- NCHS statutory authorities: cdc.gov/nchs/about/nchs-statutory-authorities.html; 42 U.S.C. §242k; NCHS "Current Legislative Authorities" (2014)
- Census Bureau NHIS page (legal authority for data collection)
- "Origin and Program of the U.S. National Health Survey" (Series A, No. 1) and "The National Health Survey — in the Beginning" (CDC Stacks)
- "Overview of the 2019 NHIS Questionnaire Redesign" (PMC10003503); 2019 and 2022 NHIS Survey Descriptions
- CDC RDC and Data Linkage pages; IPUMS NHIS user notes; Healthy People 2030 AHS-01 methodology page
- NHIS Early Release health insurance reports (2024–2025); Federal Register notice 91 FR 53869 (OMB 0920-0214 revision)

**One caveat**: I was unable to complete a final search on the most recent (2024–2026) budget and administrative developments due to search limits; the figures above for recent sample sizes and the pending OMB renewal are drawn from primary documents found earlier, but I recommend checking the NHIS site and recent Federal Register notices for the very latest status before citing in formal work.

*Assessment date: October 2026. All findings based on primary sources (CDC/NCHS documentation, OMB ICR records, Federal Register, HHS budget documents) and independent monitoring (American Statistical Association, Williams Institute, KFF, AP/Axios reporting).*

---

## 1. Historical Data Availability

**Evidence by level:**
- *Gone/High Risk*: No evidence found. No prior-year NHIS files have been removed from CDC servers.
- *Moderate Risk*: The gender identity question was removed from the survey in 2025 (pursuant to EO 14168), but this affects **future collection**, not previously released files — prior-year files containing that variable remain posted unaltered as far as can be determined.
- *No Known Issue*: Direct verification of the CDC FTP directory (ftp.cdc.gov/pub/Health_Statistics/NCHS/Dataset_Documentation/NHIS/) confirms complete annual file directories **1963 through 2025** remain publicly accessible, with no gaps. An independent, fully harmonized mirror exists via IPUMS NHIS (University of Minnesota, 1963–present).

**Assessment: No Known Issue.** Historical microdata and documentation remain fully accessible at the primary location, with a robust secondary preservation layer at IPUMS.

---

## 2. Future Data Availability

**Evidence by level:**
- *High Risk*: The ICR (OMB No. 0920-0214) has **not** lapsed — it is active through 12/31/2026, and a revision covering the 2026 NHIS has already been approved by OMB (omb.report, ICR 202609-0920-001). Collection was paused ~7 weeks (Oct 1–Nov 17, 2025) during the government shutdown but **not skipped** — the 2025 survey was completed with a shifted interview schedule.
- *Moderate Risk*: Multiple documented delays and degradations:
  - The 2025 public-use file was released in **September 2026** (NCHS blog, 2026), later than the typical August release; NCHS's 2025 Survey Description explicitly attributes "slight delays in the processing of data" to the lapse in appropriations.
  - **Quarterly Early Release health insurance estimates were discontinued** and replaced with a biannual release (SHADAC, 2025; NHIS website notice) — a permanent reduction in publication cadence of the survey's flagship policy product.
  - **NHIS-Teen was not fielded in 2025 and will not be fielded in 2026** (OMB ICR supporting statements).
- *No Known Issue*: Not supportable given the shutdown pause, delayed release, and discontinued quarterly series.

**Assessment: Moderate Risk.** Collection continues and the ICR is healthy, but publication has been measurably delayed and one recurring data product has been permanently reduced from quarterly to biannual.

---

## 3. Data Quality

**Evidence by level:**
- *High Risk*: Documented, realized reductions across all three rubric dimensions:
  - **Frequency**: Quarterly → biannual Early Release estimates (2025).
  - **Granularity/precision**: The 2025 file contains only **24,215 sample adults and 6,049 sample children against a redesigned target of ~30,000 adults** (2025 Survey Description), due to the shutdown plus "limitations on FRs' travel, hiring, and retention" — degrading subgroup reliability. The ICR also documents a "net decrease in the number of survey items" in adult and child questionnaires.
  - **Content**: Gender identity question and follow-up removed (EO 14168); NHIS-Teen dropped for 2025–2026.
- *Moderate Risk*: Would apply if reductions were only prospective; here they are already realized.
- *No Known Issue*: Contradicted by the above.

**Assessment: High Risk.** Reductions in granularity, timeliness, and frequency have already occurred and are documented in NCHS's own publications. (Mitigant: a new 2020-Census-based sample design implemented in 2025 was intended to *improve* state-level reliability, but the achieved sample fell well short of target.)

---

## 4. Statutory Context

**Evidence by level:**
- *No Known Issue*: NHIS has among the strongest statutory footings of any federal survey: authorized by the **National Health Survey Act of 1956 (P.L. 84-652)**, which mandates a *continuing* survey, and carried out under **PHS Act §306 (42 U.S.C. §242k)**. It is the designated source for numerous **Healthy People 2030 objectives** and congressionally mandated reporting. There is **no adequate substitute**: the CPS ASEC covers insurance but not the breadth of morbidity, disability, and access content; no other federal collection replicates it.
- *Moderate/High Risk*: Not applicable to the survey's own authorization. One caveat: the FY2026 President's Budget proposes **moving NCHS out of CDC into a new HHS "Office of Strategy"** — an organizational change that does not alter the underlying statutory mandate.

**Assessment: No Known Issue.** Statutory authorization is explicit, long-standing, programmatically load-bearing, and without substitutes. (This category measures legal grounding, not political safety.)

---

## 5. Staffing and Funding

**Evidence by level:**
- *High Risk*: The October 10, 2025 RIF notices to **~110 NCHS employees (~25% of the agency's workforce)** would have approached this threshold — but all NCHS RIFs were **rescinded by November 18, 2025** (AJPH 2026; American Statistical Association "Nation's Data at Risk"). No division was permanently eliminated (unlike NSDUH, PRAMS, and food-insecurity monitoring elsewhere in HHS/USDA).
- *Moderate Risk* — multiple criteria met:
  - **~10% staffing loss at NCHS by Fall 2025** even excluding the rescinded RIFs (ASA report).
  - **Budget**: FY2025 held flat at $187.4M (2.4% purchasing-power loss); **FY2026 President's Budget requests $175M — a 6.6–9% cut**, with staffing of 428 vs. 470 FTEs (COSSA analysis; ASA).
  - **Ended contracts** "particularly weakening the publication of reports and the release of data" (ASA).
  - **Threatened organizational/leadership change**: proposed transfer of NCHS from CDC to the new Office of Strategy; CDC-wide reorganization planning under the HHS "transformation" (HHS press release, March 2025; AP/PBS reporting).
- *No Known Issue*: Not supportable.

**Assessment: Moderate Risk.** Cuts sit at the low end of the Moderate band, but the October 2025 RIF episode — in which a quarter of the agency was given termination notices and only saved by the shutdown-ending spending deal — demonstrates that escalation to High Risk is a live possibility, not hypothetical.

---

## 6. Policy

**Evidence by level:**
- *High Risk*:
  - **Presidential Action-driven ICR change**: NHIS's gender identity question (and verbatim follow-up) was removed via an OMB change request **explicitly citing Executive Order 14168** ("gender ideology"), per KFF's analysis of the NHIS/MCBS/NCVS changes and the Williams Institute's February 2026 report documenting SOGI removals across ~360 federal collections. This fits the rubric's "Presidential Action-driven information collection request" criterion directly.
  - **Other significant changes in accordance with Administration priorities**: NHIS-Teen discontinued; net reduction in questionnaire items; quarterly insurance estimates ended; NCHS targeted for relocation under the administration's HHS restructuring (Office of Strategy / MAHA agenda).
- *Moderate Risk*: Would apply if changes were merely proposed; the EO-driven questionnaire change is already implemented.
- *No Known Issue*: Clearly contradicted — there have been notable changes since January 2025 affecting what data is collected.

**Assessment: High Risk.** The survey's content has already been altered by direct presidential action, with changes implemented through the ICR process (largely non-substantive change requests rather than notice-and-comment).

---

## Summary

| Category | Risk Level |
|---|---|
| Historical Data Availability | **No Known Issue** |
| Future Data Availability | **Moderate Risk** |
| Data Quality | **High Risk** |
| Statutory Context | **No Known Issue** |
| Staffing and Funding | **Moderate Risk** |
| Policy | **High Risk** |

**Overall interpretation for preservation planning:** NHIS is a paradox — legally one of the most secure federal datasets (explicit statutory mandate, no substitutes, intact historical archive back to 1963), yet operationally among the most stressed. The threats are not (so far) deletion of existing data but **forward-looking erosion**: smaller samples, fewer items, less frequent releases, EO-driven content removal, and a demonstrated willingness (October 2025 RIFs) to terminate a quarter of the parent agency's staff. Preservationists should prioritize (1) mirroring every year's questionnaire and documentation to track content changes, especially pre/post-EO 14168 instruments; (2) archiving the final quarterly Early Release series, now discontinued; and (3) capturing NHIS-Teen files and 2025 interview-period documentation, since the 2025 cycle's anomalies will complicate future analyses.
